messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room, Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Negative Appraisals: Hopelessness: I have no future, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi is a 37-year-old psychologist who came to therapy six months after he was raped by a male colleague during a professional conference. The assault occurred in the colleague’s hotel room, a space Kofi had entered willingly, believing they were meeting to discuss a collaborative research project. The door clicked shut automatically behind him, and within moments, the conversation shifted into something he could not have predicted and could not stop. He froze, his body going still as his mind scrambled to make sense of what was happening. Afterwards, he dressed in silence, walked out of the room, and flew home the next morning without telling anyone.

In the weeks that followed, Kofi found himself unable to sit in his own office at the community mental health center where he worked. The room had a door that locked from the inside, and every time he closed it to begin a session, he felt his chest tighten and his breathing grow shallow. He began leaving the door slightly ajar, then propping it open with a chair, then eventually asking a colleague if he could use a shared space instead. He told himself it was about ventilation, about needing more light. But he knew the truth: being in a locked or confined room made him feel like he was back in that hotel, and he had come to believe that he could not stop bad things from happening to him, that his body and his will were not his own. This sense of helplessness became the lens through which he saw everything. He felt that others could see what had happened to him just by looking at him, as though the assault was written on his skin. He started avoiding eye contact with male clients, especially those who reminded him of the colleague, and he began scheduling his sessions so that he was never alone in the building with another man. What frightened him most was the certainty that he had no future—that the life he had been building, the career he had worked for, was already over.

These negative appraisals fed directly into a state of constant threat. Kofi could not relax, even in places he logically knew were safe. At home, he slept on the couch with his back against the armrest, facing the door, because he felt unsafe unless his back was against a wall where he could see the room. He had difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay alert, his ears tuned to every creak and footstep. The vigilance was exhausting, but he could not let it go. He was certain that if he let his guard down, something else would happen. And this vigilance, in turn, reinforced his belief that he was fundamentally exposed and helpless. The more he scanned for danger, the more dangerous the world felt. He began to withdraw from social life entirely, declining invitations from friends and canceling plans at the last minute. His supervisor noticed that he seemed distracted and asked if everything was all right. Kofi said he was tired, and left it at that.

The threat also intensified his sensitivity to triggers. One afternoon, a female colleague mentioned a news article about sexual violence in the workplace, and Kofi felt his stomach drop. He excused himself to the restroom and stood with his hands on the sink, breathing slowly, trying to push the memory back down. Comments on sexual trauma cues had become unbearable. They pulled him into the moment of the assault with a vividness that felt like reliving it. He also found himself increasingly uncomfortable being alone with men, even those he had known for years. He started timing his arrivals and departures to avoid walking through the corridor at the same time as male coworkers. He knew this was changing how he worked, how he lived, but he could not see a way out. He had begun to believe that the assault had not only happened to him but had also revealed something true about the world—that safety was an illusion, and that he would never feel it again.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was a session with a new client, a man who spoke in a soft, measured tone that reminded him of the colleague. Kofi felt his hands go cold, his mind go blank, and for a full thirty seconds he could not speak. He ended the session early and sat in his car in the parking lot, shaking. He realized he could not keep doing this—could not keep pretending that the door was open for ventilation, could not keep arranging his life around a terror he refused to name. He was most afraid that therapy would not work, that the hopelessness was correct, that his future really was gone. But he was also afraid of what it might mean if he started to feel safe again—whether that would mean forgiving, or forgetting, or betraying what had happened. He came to the first session wanting to know if it was possible to live without the wall at his back, and not knowing if he was ready to find out.
